title: Lease
summary:
A lease is **temporary ownership that expires on its own**: `Lease(resource=X, owner=A, expires_at=10:00:10)`.

Think of a **hotel key card**: it is yours, but only until checkout. When time is up the system invalidates it without you handing it back, and the next guest gets a new card.

- The holder must **renew** before expiry to keep ownership; if it crashes or is partitioned, the lease simply lapses and someone else can take over. That is the point: no one has to detect the failure for ownership to move.
- Expiry gives **liveness** (the resource is never stuck), not **safety**: a paused holder can wake up and act on an expired lease. Pair leases with a [fencing token](#/sd/f/fencing-token).
- **Who grants leases?** Only the single owner of the state machine (the orchestrator). Middleware in between — a dispatcher, a gateway, a message queue — passes work along but must never *own* the lease.

drills.q: A worker holds a 30 s lease on a job and crashes without saying anything. What happens to the job?
options: It stays stuck until an operator releases the lease
The lease expires after at most 30 s and the job can be granted to another worker
The lock service immediately detects the crash and reassigns the job
The job is lost unless the worker wrote a checkpoint
drills.explain: Expiry is the whole mechanism: nobody has to detect the crash. The worst case is waiting out the remaining lease time.

drills.q: What does a lease guarantee on its own?
options: Liveness: ownership cannot be stuck forever
Safety: two holders can never act on the resource at the same time
drills.explain: A holder paused by GC or the network can resume after its lease expired and still act. Safety needs the resource to reject stale holders — a **fencing token**.

drills.q: In a job system with an orchestrator, a dispatch service, a worker gateway and a message queue, which component should own the job leases?
options: The message queue, since it delivers the job
The dispatch service, since it picks the worker
The orchestrator, the single owner of the job state machine
Each worker, for the jobs it runs
drills.explain: Lease authority belongs to whoever exclusively owns the state machine. Middleware forwards work; letting it own leases splits the source of truth.

drills.q: A worker renews its lease every 10 s. The lease lasts 30 s. If the worker crashes right after a renewal, how many seconds until another worker can take the job, at most?
drills.explain: Takeover waits for the full lease after the last renewal: 30 s. This is the trade-off — longer leases tolerate hiccups, shorter leases fail over faster.

drills.q: Put a lease's life cycle in order.
items: The owner asks the lease authority for a lease on the resource
The authority grants it with an expiry time
The owner renews before expiry while it keeps working
The owner stops renewing (crash, pause or done)
The lease expires and the resource can be granted again
drills.explain: Grant → renew → stop renewing → expire. Release is an optimization; expiry is what makes it safe to assume the owner is gone.

drills.q: Explain a lease to an interviewer in two sentences, with an analogy.
drills.answer: A lease is ownership with a built-in expiry: the holder keeps it only by renewing, so if it dies the ownership frees itself. Like a hotel key card that stops working at checkout without you returning it.
